strengths: The unified representation of objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances addresses an important limitation of object-centric 3D scene graphs and is well motivated for embodied AI.

OP3DSG is a coherent end-to-end system combining part-specialized open-vocabulary detection, multi-view fusion, geometric graph initialization, and decomposed LLM reasoning. The geometry-first design is sensible and practically motivated.

The reported gains under the primary protocol are large: overall node R@3 increases to 84.1 from 60.6, while functional and spatial triplet R@3 reach 51.1 and 52.4. The component ablations also show substantial, interpretable changes.

UniGraph3D moves toward a useful joint evaluation setting by consolidating existing resources and adding object-part connectivity and affordances. The paper is generally clear, visually polished, and includes both quantitative and qualitative results.

The real-robot demonstrations illustrate the potential utility of unified graphs for question answering, planning, retrieval, and navigation, even though they do not yet constitute rigorous downstream evaluation.
weaknesses: The primary metric is too permissive for a 3D grounding claim: a prediction needs only non-zero 3D IoU, followed by top-K embedding retrieval. Under stricter localization in Table 4, OP3DSG is worse than KeySG on part nodes (25.8 versus 30.4 at IoU>=0.10 and 13.0 versus 23.4 at IoP>=0.25). Thus the headline part-node advantage largely does not establish accurate part localization.

All main graph results report recall without precision, F1, or average precision. This is particularly problematic because the method claims that verification suppresses spurious edges and improves precision. Affordance recall is additionally evaluated independently of node correctness, so generic or over-produced predictions may score well. The evidence therefore cannot substantiate the central hallucination-reduction claim.

The benchmark description is insufficient for judging reliability or reproducibility. It contains only 251 object nodes and 414 part nodes, while the manuscript does not specify the number of scenes, splits, annotator count, agreement, quality-control protocol, label distributions, or release/licensing plan. Evaluation on a small consolidation of existing datasets also leaves generalization unclear.

Important implementation details are missing: the curated object-part knowledge base and its coverage, all association and geometry thresholds, color-feature weights, remote-candidate selection, exact prompts, verification procedure, LLM decoding settings, and run-to-run variability. Equation 1 also does not match the stated specular-pixel exclusion: the complement of low-saturation-and-overexposed is an OR condition, whereas the displayed valid-set predicate uses an AND condition.

The claimed open-vocabulary capability is qualified by a manually curated object-part knowledge base and lexical containment heuristic. Coverage of unseen objects, synonymous part names, unusual object-part compositions, and domain shifts is not evaluated.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because the authors retrofit methods with their own unspecified LLM prompts, while OP3DSG also uses a part-specialized detector. There are no oracle-node or controlled-detector experiments separating gains from perception, graph reasoning, and stronger prior knowledge.
Claims of efficiency and scalability are unsupported: no runtime, memory, token usage, API cost, number-of-node scaling study, or comparison with VLM-based inference is reported.

The robot section is anecdotal. It provides no number of environments or trials, task-success rates, localization/navigation metrics, failure analysis, or controlled comparison. Consequently, claims that OP3DSG is a robust perception backbone for real-world tasks are substantially stronger than the supplied evidence.

No contribution type is declared, so I assess this primarily as Algorithms/General with a secondary Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. The integration is useful, but the algorithmic ingredients are mostly established models, classical color histograms, greedy fusion, heuristics, and LLM prompting; the current evaluation is not rigorous enough to make the combined system or benchmark a convincing ECCV contribution.

The pipeline is conceptually coherent: object-part knowledge expands candidate prompts, color cues augment multi-view part association, and geometric structure constrains subsequent language-model reasoning.

The paper reports substantial gains on its proposed benchmark and includes component ablations. In particular, removing object-part knowledge or splitting the LLM roles causes large decreases, suggesting that these design choices matter within the reported setup.
Consolidating functional-scene datasets and adding object-part, relation, and affordance annotations could provide a useful starting point for studying unified 3D scene graphs.
weaknesses: Using the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the central empirical case is not sufficiently reliable. The main node metric accepts any nonzero 3D IoU, an exceptionally permissive localization condition. Under the more meaningful thresholds in Table 4, part localization is weak: OP3DSG obtains 25.8/13.0 for IoU>=0.10/IoP>=0.25, below KeySG's 30.4/23.4. This sharply qualifies the headline part-node R@3 of 83.6 and does not convincingly support claims of accurate fine-grained grounding.

All principal graph metrics report recall only. They therefore do not measure false-positive nodes, edges, or affordances, despite the paper's central claim that geometry and verification suppress spurious predictions and hallucinations. Precision, F1, graph-level exactness, and calibration are needed; recall alone can improve through overprediction.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently defined and potentially semantically permissive. Node and relation correctness relies on embedding similarity and top-K ranking, but the candidate universe, ranking procedure, thresholds, handling of duplicate predictions, and matching policy are not specified. Affordance recall is explicitly computed independently of the associated node, so a correct phrase attached to the wrong entity may receive credit.

UniGraph3D is small—251 object nodes, 414 part nodes, 357 spatial edges, and 425 functional edges—and is derived from only two existing resources. The supplied manuscript does not report the number of scenes or splits, annotator counts, agreement, quality-control results, label distributions, or independence between benchmark annotation and the empirically curated object-part knowledge base. These omissions make generalization and leakage difficult to assess.

The comparison conflates several factors. OP3DSG uses a dedicated part-segmentation model pretrained on part-centric datasets, while baselines are retrofitted by the authors using unspecified prompts. There is no controlled comparison using the same detector and node proposals, nor an oracle-node experiment isolating graph reasoning. Consequently, the large gains cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed fusion or geometry-gated reasoning.

Important implementation details are absent: the object-part knowledge base and its coverage, association thresholds and weights, spatial-relation rules, remote-candidate selection, verification-gate criteria, complete prompts, decoding settings, number of runs, and variance. Dependence on a proprietary dated GPT-5 model further raises reproducibility concerns. Even the color filtering is internally inconsistent: Eq. (1) keeps pixels satisfying S>tau_S and V<tau_V, which does not match the stated operation of excluding only simultaneously weak-chromatic and overexposed pixels.

The scalability and efficiency motivation is not experimentally tested. There are no runtime, memory, token, cost, graph-size scaling, or comparison measurements, despite repeated claims that the split-agent design avoids quadratic inference and context overload.

The robot section is qualitative rather than an evaluation: it provides no number of trials, task success rates, scene diversity, failure analysis, latency, or baseline comparison. It therefore does not support claims that OP3DSG is a robust perception backbone for navigation and task planning.

The technical novelty is limited at the component level: the method largely assembles an existing image tagger, a pretrained part detector, conventional multi-view fusion and color histograms, geometric heuristics, and prompted LLM agents. A unified formulation may still be valuable, but stronger evaluation and substantially clearer algorithmic specification are necessary to establish the claimed contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies an important gap between object-centric spatial 3D scene graphs and function-centric representations, and the proposed unified graph—objects, parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances—is well motivated for embodied applications.

OP3DSG is a coherent, training-free integration of part-aware detection, multi-view fusion, geometric priors, and decomposed LLM reasoning. The object-conditioned part vocabulary and color-assisted part association are simple, practical ideas.

Results on UniGraph3D show large improvements under the primary retrieval protocol: overall-node R@3 rises to 84.1 from 60.6 for the strongest baseline, while functional- and spatial-triplet R@3 reach 51.1 and 52.4. Component ablations indicate that knowledge-guided candidates, color features, the prior graph, and agent decomposition all contribute.

The per-source-dataset results and evaluation on the object-centric ReplicaSSG benchmark provide some evidence that the gains are not solely an artifact of merging datasets. The efficiency comparison also suggests substantially fewer VLM/LLM calls than caption-based baselines.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, and its qualitative analysis candidly identifies failures from occlusion, reflections, fragmentation, and thin-object confusion.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The technical novelty is modest: most components are established models or standard techniques—RAM, VLPart, SAM, color histograms, greedy fusion, geometric heuristics, and LLM prompting. The main novelty is their integration and task formulation rather than a new learning or inference method.

The primary node metric accepts any non-zero 3D IoU, which is too permissive to establish accurate part grounding. Under the more meaningful localization thresholds in Table 4, OP3DSG's part performance is only 25.8 at IoU>=0.10 and 13.0 at IoP>=0.25, below KeySG's 30.4 and 23.4. This materially qualifies the headline claim of substantially improved fine-grained part localization.

Evaluation reports recall almost exclusively, despite repeatedly claiming that the method suppresses spurious edges and hallucinations. Precision, F1, graph-level false-positive rates, and calibration are absent. This is especially problematic for affordances, whose metric is explicitly independent of the associated node; together with the severe label imbalance visible in Fig. 7, this calls for frequency baselines and per-class metrics.

UniGraph3D is small—251 object nodes, 414 part nodes, 357 spatial edges, 425 functional edges, and 554 affordance annotations—and mostly consolidates two existing resources. The paper does not adequately specify scene splits, annotator counts, quality-control procedures, inter-annotator agreement, or how hyperparameters were selected without overfitting to this benchmark.

The claimed open-vocabulary capability is insufficiently validated. Part candidates come from an empirically curated object-part knowledge base and a detector pretrained on LVIS/PACO, but the knowledge-base contents and coverage are not provided and there is no evaluation on unseen objects, unseen parts, or novel compositions. An object absent from the predefined knowledge base may not receive part prompts, so the claim that this mechanism preserves open-vocabulary part recognition needs qualification.

Reproducibility is limited: the prompts and exact verification-gate logic are omitted; several association thresholds and remote-candidate selection rules are unspecified; the knowledge base is unavailable; and LLM decoding settings, run-to-run variance, latency, and monetary cost are not reported. Results based on a proprietary GPT-5 snapshot therefore cannot currently be independently reproduced.

The robot section is only a qualitative demonstration. It provides no number of scenes or trials, task-success rates, localization/navigation accuracy, comparison against simpler graph representations, or controlled evidence that part-aware graphs improve downstream performance. Thus claims that OP3DSG is a robust backbone for diverse real-world robotics tasks are stronger than the presented evidence.

The work is promising and close to the acceptance boundary, but the permissive main metric, lack of precision-based evaluation, underspecified benchmark/LLM protocol, and absence of quantitative robotic validation leave the central claims about accurate, hallucination-resistant, and practically useful unified graphs insufficiently established.

The proposed pipeline is intuitively structured. Part-aware detection, multi-view fusion using geometric/semantic/color evidence, a geometry-derived prior graph, and separate LLM roles form a plausible practical system.

Reported recall improvements are large, and the paper includes component ablations, stricter localization measurements, per-source-dataset results, an object-centric ReplicaSSG experiment, qualitative failure cases, and a limited efficiency analysis.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful overview figures and a readable explanation of the intended representation.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the empirical case is not sufficiently reliable. The primary metrics use an extremely permissive non-zero 3D-IoU localization requirement and embedding-based top-k semantic matching. No precision, false-positive, graph-level, or calibration metric is reported. Consequently, predicting many nodes, edges, or common labels can increase recall without producing an accurate graph. This is especially problematic because the paper repeatedly claims suppression of spurious relations and hallucinations—claims that recall alone cannot establish.

The stricter localization results substantially weaken the headline part-grounding claim. At IoU>=0.10, OP3DSG obtains 25.8 part-node recall versus KeySG's 30.4; at IoP>=0.25, it obtains 13.0 versus 23.4. Its overall IoP result, 31.4, is also below KeySG's 37.0. Thus, the very large gains under the non-zero-overlap protocol do not translate to superior fine-grained part localization.

UniGraph3D is small—251 object nodes, 414 part nodes, 357 spatial edges, and 425 functional edges—and is assembled from only two existing resources. The paper does not provide essential annotation details such as the number and expertise of annotators, independent labeling, agreement, adjudication, quality-control statistics, scene splits, or measures against benchmark-specific tuning. Figure 7 also shows severe class imbalance, yet no macro or per-class results are reported.

The comparison is not sufficiently diagnostic or demonstrably fair. Most baselines were designed for object-centric or functional graphs and are retrofitted with author-designed, insufficiently documented LLM prompts, whereas OP3DSG directly uses VLPart pretrained on part-centric LVIS/PACO data plus a curated object-part knowledge base. There is no comparison to a strong part-segmentation/lifting pipeline using methods cited by the paper, so the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed fusion and reasoning design.

The open-vocabulary claim is overstated for parts. Part candidates are retrieved from a finite, empirically curated object-part knowledge base, and object-part attachment relies on the object label literally occurring in the conditioned part label. The knowledge base, its coverage, and behavior for unseen objects or parts are not disclosed or evaluated. This is controlled-vocabulary candidate expansion downstream of open-vocabulary object tagging, rather than convincingly open-vocabulary part discovery.

Critical implementation details are missing: the knowledge-base contents, association thresholds, exact nearest-neighbor-ratio definition, spatial-relation rules, remote-candidate selection, verification-gate logic, prompts, output parsing, decoding settings, and repeated-run variance. The project-page field is blank, and reliance on a proprietary GPT-5 snapshot further limits reproducibility. Equation 1 is also inconsistent with its prose: excluding pixels that are simultaneously bright and weakly chromatic requires an OR in the retained-set complement, whereas the equation uses AND.

The claimed real-world robotics impact is supported only by illustrations and qualitative demonstrations. There are no task counts, success rates, repetitions, baselines, latency measurements, or controlled comparisons for question answering, navigation, or task planning. The system is therefore not shown to be a robust perception backbone for these tasks.

The efficiency and scalability evidence is incomplete. The paper reports only detector-stage peak GPU memory and approximate numbers of model calls, excludes baseline VLM memory, gives OP3DSG's LLM calls merely as '>3,' and omits runtime, token usage, API cost, graph size scaling, and context-length behavior. This does not substantiate the claimed scalability advantage.

The technical novelty is modest relative to the breadth of the claims: much of the system composes existing RAM, VLPart, SAM, heuristic online fusion, hand-built geometric rules, and several LLM prompts. The ablation results show that the curated knowledge base and prompt decomposition drive much of the improvement, but the current evaluation does not establish that these components generalize beyond the narrowly constructed benchmark.

strengths: The paper tackles an important gap in embodied 3D understanding: existing scene graphs generally model either object-level spatial structure or part-level functionality, whereas OP3DSG jointly represents objects, interactive parts, spatial and functional relations, and affordances. This unified formulation is well motivated and potentially useful for robotics.

The proposed pipeline is technically coherent. Knowledge-guided part prompting addresses missed small components, color-aware multi-view fusion targets unstable part association, and the geometry-initialized graph constrains LLM reasoning. These components address identifiable failure modes rather than being an arbitrary collection of modules.

The empirical improvements are substantial. On UniGraph3D, OP3DSG reaches 84.1/88.9 overall-node R@3/R@5 and 51.1/64.5 functional-triplet recall, markedly exceeding the reported baselines. The component ablations are informative: removing knowledge guidance, color features, the prior graph, or agent specialization produces consistent degradation.

Evaluation on the separate source datasets and the object-centric ReplicaSSG benchmark provides some evidence that the gains are not solely an artifact of merging datasets. The efficiency analysis and real-robot demonstrations further support the practical relevance of the approach.

The manuscript is clearly organized and visually communicates the unified representation well. It also includes useful qualitative failure cases involving occlusion, reflections, fragmentation, and thin-object confusion.
weaknesses: The main evaluation relies almost exclusively on recall. This is particularly problematic for an LLM-based graph generator that claims to suppress hallucinated or spurious edges: a method could increase recall by producing many nodes, relations, or affordances. Precision, F1, graph-level accuracy, calibration, or explicit false-positive statistics are needed to substantiate the verification-gate claims.

The primary node protocol is permissive, requiring only non-zero 3D IoU. Under stricter localization criteria, part performance drops sharply to 25.8 R@3 at IoU>=0.10 and 13.0 at IoP>=0.25; it is also below KeySG's 30.4 and 23.4 on these respective part metrics. Thus, the very high 83.6 part-node R@3 in the main table should not be interpreted as equally strong geometric localization.

The claimed open-vocabulary generality is only partially established. Part candidates come from an empirically curated object-part knowledge base, and object-part attachment uses lexical containment aligned with those generated labels. The paper does not report knowledge-base size and coverage, performance on unseen object-part combinations, sensitivity to missing or incorrect entries, or generalization to parts outside the curated vocabulary.

Reproducibility is limited. The exact knowledge base, full LLM prompts, remote-candidate selection procedure, verification rules, several association thresholds, annotation instructions, annotator agreement, and stochastic-run variance are not provided. Reliance on the proprietary GPT-5-2025-08-07 model further makes exact replication difficult.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. OP3DSG uses a dedicated part detector pretrained on LVIS and PACO, whereas object-centric baselines are retrofitted through prompting. Comparisons against stronger part-segmentation-and-lifting systems, and controlled baselines using the same detector and LLM with alternative fusion or graph construction, would better isolate the proposed contributions.

UniGraph3D is useful but modest in scale, with 251 object nodes and 414 part nodes, and is derived from two existing datasets. More detail is needed about scene counts, splits, annotation quality control, and whether design choices such as label consolidation favor the proposed prompting and evaluation pipeline.

The downstream robot section is qualitative: it provides examples of question answering, planning, querying, and navigation but no number of trials, task-success rate, comparison baseline, or failure statistics. Consequently, the claim that OP3DSG is a robust backbone for diverse real-world tasks is promising but not quantitatively demonstrated. Overall, the formulation and strong results merit a slight preference for acceptance, but the recall-only evaluation and incomplete reproducibility prevent a stronger score.
